blocks.text: Have you ever wondered why your soap doesn't lather well in certain types of water?

blocks.markdown: In this lesson, we will explore how soap is made, why it behaves differently in hard water, and the advantages of detergents over soap.

blocks.title: Definition of Soap
blocks.text: Soap is a salt of a fatty acid, typically made by the chemical reaction between fats and an alkali.

blocks.markdown: Soap is traditionally made through a process called saponification. This involves heating fats or oils with a strong alkali, such as sodium hydroxide (NaOH). The reaction produces soap and glycerol as by-products.

blocks.title: Making Soap
blocks.prompt: Outline the process of making soap from fat and alkali.

steps.text: Start with a fat or oil, such as palm oil.
Add a strong alkali, like sodium hydroxide (NaOH), to the fat.
Heat the mixture to initiate the saponification reaction.
Allow the reaction to produce soap and glycerol.

blocks.answer: Soap is made by heating fats or oils with sodium hydroxide, resulting in soap and glycerol.

blocks.markdown: Soap tends to lather poorly in hard water due to the presence of calcium and magnesium ions. These ions react with soap to form insoluble salts, reducing its effectiveness.

blocks.title: Exam Tip
blocks.text: Remember, detergents do not form insoluble salts in hard water, making them more effective than soap in such conditions.

points: Soap is made by reacting fats with an alkali, a process known as saponification.
Soap lathers poorly in hard water due to the formation of insoluble salts.
Detergents are more effective in hard water as they do not form insoluble salts.
